evidence: createApp: creates InMemoryProductRepository/InMemoryOrderRepository and CatalogueService/OrderService — composition-root wiring, which fits infrastructure
Route handlers delegate to catalogue.addProduct, orderService.placeOrder, listOrders, cancelOrder, advanceOrder with no business logic in between
GET /orders: isOrderStatus(state) check returns 400 — checks transport input
POST /orders/:id/:action: maps the 'cancel' and status actions to service calls; rejecting 'placed' is a check on route parameters, while transitions appear to be left to the service/domain
sendError: maps DomainError to 400 and anything else to 500 — HTTP error translation
startServer: reads process.env.PORT and calls listen — framework/runtime concern
parsedVerdict.reasoning: HttpServer.ts is an infrastructure HTTP adapter plus composition root. Its jobs are: wiring repositories and services (createApp), Express routing that hands work straight to application services, checking transport input (isOrderStatus on the query and route parameters), turning errors into HTTP status codes (sendError), and starting the server (startServer). It holds no persistence logic and no business rules. Rejecting the 'placed' action is a borderline case. In context it maps URL actions to service commands and gives a 400 for an action the API doesn't offer. Order-transition rules appear to be enforced through OrderService.advanceOrder and DomainError, but those files weren't provided, so I couldn't confirm it. Overall, every responsibility fits the infrastructure layer.
